Six had myoclonus of various etiologies and one each had progressive supranuclear palsy, Filipino X-linked dystonia with parkinsonism, painful legs and moving toes, and stiff-person syndrome. Milacemide was initiated at a dose of 2,400 mg/day, orally, and increased gradually to a maximum of 4,800 mg/day. No clear-cut observable improvement occurred. There were no serious adverse effects.

Vol. 8, No. 4, 1993, pp. 484-488.

Therapeutic Trial of Milacemide in Patients With 
Myoclonus and Other Intractable Movement Disorders 
Mark Forrest Gordon, Roland0 Diaz-Olivo, Ann L. Hunt, and Stanley Fahn 
Department of Neurology. The Neurological Institute, Columbia-Presbyterian Medical Center, 
New York, New York, U.S.A. 
Summary: We performed a therapeutic trial with the glycine precursor, mila- 
cemide, on 10 patients with intractable movement disorders. Six had myoclo- 
nus of various etiologies and one each had progressive supranuclear palsy, 
Filipino X-linked dystonia with parkinsonism, painful legs and moving toes, 
and stiff-person syndrome. Milacemide was initiated at a dose of 2,400 mg/day, 
orally, and increased gradually to a maximum of 4,800 mg/day. No clear-cut 
observable improvement occurred. There were no serious adverse effects. Key 
Words: Milacemide-Glycine-Myoclonus-Stiff-person syndrome-X-linked 
dystonia-Progressive supranuclear palsy-Cortical-basal ganglionic degener- 
ation-Striatonigral degeneration. 
Myoclonus refers to sudden, brief, shock-like in- 
voluntary movements caused by active muscle con- 
tractions (positive myoclonus) or by sudden, brief 
lapses of tonic contraction in active postural mus- 
cles (negative myoclonus) (1). Current therapy for 
myoclonus is often not satisfactory. Treatments 
may include clonazepam, valproic acid, primidone, 
and L-5-hydroxytryptophan (L-5-HTP) with carbi- 
dopa (to prevent peripheral decarboxylation). In ad- 
dition, piracetam, fluoxetine, clomipramine, dopa- 
mine or dopamine agonists, opiates (codeine), tri- 
hexyphenidyl, carbamazepine, and tetrabenazine 
have occasionally been beneficial. Specific thera- 
pies for the various types of myoclonus have not 
been delineated. Epileptic and cortical myoclonus 
may respond best to anticonvulsants, such as clo- 
nazepam, valproic acid, and primidone. 
The brainstem and spinal cord inhibitory neuro- 
transmitter, glycine, has been implicated in the 
pathophysiology of myoclonus. Stereotactic infu- 
sion of the glycine receptor antagonist, strychnine, 
into the medullary reticular formation induces gen- 
Address correspondence and reprint requests to Dr. s. Fahn, 
Neurological Institute, 710 West 168th Street, New York, NY 
10032-3784, U.S.A. 
eralized stimulus-sensitive myoclonus in the rat (2). 
The glycine receptor is involved in urea-induced 
myoclonus (3). Whole-brain and brainstem glycine 
levels are decreased in DDT-induced myoclonus in 
mice and rats (43). Intraventricular glycine sup- 
presses DDT-induced myoclonus (6). 
Animal models of myoclonus, implicating glycin- 
ergic dysfunction led Truong and Fahn (7) to try 
glycine in patients with myoclonus; however, gly- 
cine in doses up to 6 g/day was unsuccessful in the 
treatment of myoclonus. CSF glycine levels did not 
change during treatment; this finding suggested that 
this dose did not effectively enter the brain. Animal 
studies had previously shown that glycine does not 
easily cross the blood-brain barrier (8,9). 
Milacemide (2-n-pentylaminoacetamide), rnanu- 
factured by Searle, is a prodrug of glycine. Milace- 
mide readily penetrates the blood-brain barrier; in 
the brain; it is metabolized by monoamine oxi- 
dase-B (MAO-B) to glycineamide and then to gly- 
cine (10). In rats, systemic administration of mila- 
cemide blocks the myoclonus induced by DDT (1 1) 
as effectively as glycine infused into the ventricles 
(6). Glycine levels in the brain increase with admin- 
istration of milacemide, but serine levels do not 
change. Therefore, increasing brain glycine levels, 
484

MILACEMIDE IN MYOCLONUS 485 
either by systemic administration of milacemide or 
by intraventricular infusion of glycine, may be a 
mechanism to produce an antimyoclonic effect. It is 
not clear if milacemide, while preventing myoclo- 
nus in the DDT model, could also do so via seroto- 
nin neurotransmission since it inhibits MAO-B ac- 
tivity (12-14). Milacemide also increases y-ami- 
nobutyric acid (GABA) concentrations in the 
substantia nigra (10). 
Milacemide has an acceptable safety profile in 
animals (10). In humans, milacemide has been eval- 
uated for safety in healthy volunteers. Milacemide 
has been relatively well-tolerated in therapeutic tri- 
als conducted in patients with epilepsy (15). Ad- 
verse effects may include vasomotor disorders 
(flushing), nausea and vomiting, palpitations, and 
elevations in hepatic transaminases (10). These ab- 
normalities generally return to normal following 
cessation of drug or reduction of dosage (10). 
Since glycine, GABA, and the monoamines are 
major inhibitory neurotransmitters in the CNS, mi- 
lacemide may be a potential agent in the therapy of 
myoclonus and other movement disorders. Brown 
et al. (16), in an open-label trial of milacemide ti- 
trated to 2,400 mglday in seven subjects with my- 
oclonus and three with stiff-person syndrome, 
found no significant improvement. We report a trial 
of milacemide in nine patients with intractable 
movement disorders. 
METHODS 
Milacemide was obtained from Searle (Skokie, 
IL, U.S.A.). The study was approved by the Insti- 
tutional Review Board, and written informed con- 
sent was obtained from each subject enrolled. 
The study had three phases. Phase I was an open- 
label dose-titration lead-in, beginning at a dosage of 
800 mg, orally, three times a day, and not exceeding 
1,600 mg three times a day (4,800 mglday). During 
Phase I, patients who did not respond or who ex- 
perienced significant treatment-related adverse 
events were withdrawn. Phase I1 was a double- 
blind, randomized design that employed the optimal 
dose determined in Phase I or a matching placebo at 
the same dose. Subjects were transferred immedi- 
ately from Phase I to Phase 11, without gradual 
withdrawal of drug. Phase 111 was similar to Phase 
11, without gradual withdrawal of drug. Phase 111 
was similar to Phase 11, with the blinded treatment 
reversed. The study was terminated when the max- 
imal duration of treatment in Phase I11 was attained. 
Subjects could participate as inpatients or outpa- 
tients. In Phase I, dose titration occurred over 12 
days for inpatients and over 21 days for outpatients, 
followed by 1 week of treatment at the optimal 
dose. In Phase I1 and Phase 111, inpatients received 
milacemide or placebo for 1 week and outpatients 
received milacemide or placebo for 3 weeks. 
Potential subjects were men or nonpregnant 
women (either sterile or using adequate contracep- 
tives) between the ages of 18 and 90 years who suf- 
fered from myoclonus or another intractable move- 
ment disorder and who were otherwise in good 
health. For at least 30 days before enrollment, sub- 
jects were on a stable regimen of any drugs used to 
treat their myoclonus or other movement disorder. 
Patients with serious medical conditions or labora- 
tory abnormalities, recent histories of alcohol or 
drug abuse, other concurrent or recent investiga- 
tional drug studies, known hypersensitivity to mi- 
lacemide, or previous participation in this study 
were excluded. 
Screening was performed within 14 days of en- 
rollment and included informed consent, medical 
history, physical and neurologic examination, elec- 
trocardiogram, laboratory tests (complete blood 
count, electrolytes, liver functions, urine analysis, 
and pregnancy test), videotape, and assessment of 
severity. Global assessment was on a four-point 
scale: 0, no signs; 1, mild signs, not interfering with 
activities; 2, moderate signs, interfering with some 
activities; 3, severe signs, interfering with many ac- 
tivities; and 4, marked signs, interfering with most 
activities. Ratings were done by the subjects, family 
members, and treating physicians. Laboratories 
tests were repeated during the study and obtained at 
the end of each phase. 
Ten subjects were enrolled: six with myoclonus 
of various etiologies and four others with intracta- 
ble movement disorders (one each with progressive 
supranuclear palsy, Filipino x-linked dystonia with 
parkinsonism, painful legs and moving toes, and 
stiff-person syndrome; Table 1). 
CASE REPORTS 
Case 1 
A 40-year-old man with rhythmic segmental my- 
oclonus of the right arm and neck, which began at 
age 16, has a history of congenital right hemiparesis 
and hemiatrophy and seizures treated with phenyt- 
oin, 400 mg/day, and phenobarbital, 200 mg/day. 
His clinical picture has been described previously 
(17).

Case 2 
A 67-year-old woman has posthypoxic action my- 
oclonus that developed following respiratory ob- 
struction and prolonged coma. Her clinical picture 
has been described previously (18,19). 
Case 3 
A 35-year-old man with essential oscillatory my- 
oclonus beginning at about age 20 has had partial 
benefit on clonazepam, 3 mgtday, and baclofen, 60 
mglday. His clinical picture has been described pre- 
viously (20). 
Case 4 
A 21-year-old man with childhood onset of pro- 
gressive action myoclonus and ataxia, coupled with 
a few seizures that are well-controlled, carries a 
diagnosis of Ramsay Hunt syndrome. His treatment 
has included clonazepam, 1 mg; valproic acid, 500 
mg; and acetazolamide, 750 mgtday. 
Case 5 
A 64-year-old woman has progressive dystonia, 
parkinsonism, and myoclonus. Her diagnosis is un- 
known, but it is presumed to be striatonigral degen- 
eration. She receives concurrent treatment with 
clonazepam, 5.5 mg; primidone, 62.5 mg; carba- 
mazepine, 300 mg; carbidopa, 67.5 mg, and levodo- 
pa 250 mg; and protriptyline, 30 mg/day. 
Case 6 
A 71-year-old man has a 3-year history of pro- 
gressive tremulousness, stiffness, slowness, and 
fixed dystonic posturing of his right arm; the trem- 
ulousness is continual myoclonic jerks. He did not 
respond to high-dose levodopa. His presumed diag- 
nosis was cortical-basal ganglionic degeneration, 
and he takes clonazepam, 1.5 mg/day. 
Case 7 
A 57-year-old woman has a few-year history of 
progressive parkinsonism, retrocollis, and ophthal- 
moparesis; she is presumed to have progressive su- 
pranuclear palsy. Her treatment has included aman- 
tadine, 200 mg; selegiline, 10 mg; and imipramine, 
150 mglday . 
Case 8 
A 39-year-old Filipino man with X-linked dysto- 
nia-parkinsonism has severe freezing of gait. His 
treatment has included diazepam, 30 mg; tri- 
hexyphenidyl, 30 mg; and carbidopa, 75 mg, and 
levodopa, 300 mglday . 
Case 9 
A 68-year-old woman has a 17-year history of 
painful legs and moving toes. She is troubled by 
severe pain, which has been refractory to multiple 
therapies. 
Case 10 
A 62-year-old woman with stiff-person syndrome 
has a 5-year history of progressive stiffness and in- 
termittent muscle spasms in her lower back and 
proximal legs, responding partially to valproic acid, 
1,500 mgtday, and diazepam, 30 mgtday. She also 
has a history of pernicious anemia, treated with i.m. 
vitamin B,,, and diabetes mellitus. Antibodies were 
present in her serum against glutamic acid decar- 
boxylase, gastric parietal cells, pancreatic islet 
cells, and microsomal fraction of the thyroid.

MILACEMIDE IN MYOCLONUS 487 
RESULTS 
The clinical rating score did not change signifi- 
cantly in nine patients treated with milacemide. 
Only one (case 6, with presumed cortical-basal gan- 
glionic degeneration) had some apparent benefit 
with less severe myoclonus in the open-label trial. 
He continued through Phase I1 and Phase I11 with- 
out clear benefit. 
Eight of the I0 subjects completed Phase I (the 
open trial) to a maximum dose of 4,800 mglday. 
Two patients withdrew from the study due to side 
effects at 3,600 mglday without any benefit. A pa- 
tient (case 3) with rhythmic myoclonus experienced 
excessive appetite. The patient (case 8) with painful 
legs and moving toes had a transient exacerbation 
of her condition. Both side effects resolved after 
discontinuation of milacemide. 
Full blood counts, electrolytes, and liver function 
tests did not change significantly. 
DISCUSSION 
The 10 subjects in our study did not benefit from 
milacemide in doses up to 4,800 mg/day. Brown et 
al. (16), in an open-label trial of milacemide titrated 
to 2,400 mg/day in seven subjects with myoclonus 
and three with stiff-man syndrome, also found no 
significant improvement. 
The inhibitory neurotransmitter, glycine, was un- 
successful in the treatment of myoclonus in doses 
up to 6 g/day (7), possibly due to poor penetration of 
glycine into the brain from the peripheral circula- 
tion. However, milacemide, a glycine precursor 
known to readily cross the blood-brain barrier, did 
not improve the myoclonus in the six myoclonus 
patients in this study or in the seven patients pre- 
viously studied (16). It is possible that the dose of 
milacemide was too low to sufficiently increase gly- 
cine levels in the CNS. However, the ineffective- 
ness of milacemide in these cases of myoclonus 
may suggest that defective glycinergic neurotrans- 
mission is not an important factor in myoclonus. 
Precise mechanisms for the various types of myoc- 
lonus are not known. Posthypoxic myoclonus may 
involve serotonergic (21,22) and GABA-ergic (23) 
neurotransmission, as suggested by reduced CSF 
levels of 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (SHIAA), the 
major metabolite of serotonin, and of GABA. Post- 
anoxic myoclonus improves with drugs that en- 
hance serotonin activity [such as L-~-HTP, the im- 
mediate synthetic precursor to serotonin; tryp- 
tophan with a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (22); or 
fluoxetine, an inhibitor of serotonin reuptake (24)] 
and also with drugs, such as valproic acid and clo- 
nazepam, that enhance GABA-ergic inhibitory in- 
fluence (21,25). 
Brown et al. (16) postulated that the discrepancy 
between the effectiveness of glycine and milace- 
mide in improving DDT-induced myoclonus and 
their ineffectiveness in treating myoclonus in hu- 
mans may be due to the fact that animal experi- 
ments for myoclonus involve manipulation of the 
reticular formation and thus may not be an appro- 
priate model for cortical and spinal myoclonus. 
However, our case 2 is believed to have reticular 
reflex myoclonus (18), and she failed to improve. 
Defective glycinergic systems have been impli- 
cated in some animal models of spinal rigidity 
(26,27). Schmidt et al. (28) noted that the rigidity in 
stiff-person syndrome resembles that produced by 
strychnine poisoning and experimental cord isch- 
emia, both of which are associated with a loss of 
normal glycinergic inhibition to motoneurons from 
spinal interneurons. This observation provoked 
speculation that abnormalities in glycinergic inhibi- 
tion by spinal interneurons might play a role in stiff- 
person syndrome (28). Trials of glycine in stiff- 
person syndrome (28,29) were not successful, 
possibly because of the poor penetration of the 
blood-brain barrier by glycine (7). 
There is more evidence for an imbalance in the 
GABA-ergic system in stiff-person syndrome. Med- 
ications with GABA-ergic properties, such as diaz- 
epam (30), valproic acid (31), clonazepam (32), and 
baclofen (33,34), are beneficial in some patients. 
Antibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase, the 
enzyme that synthesizes GABA, are present in the 
serum and CSF of many stiff-person patients 
(35,36). 
We offer two possible explanations for the lack of 
benefit in subjects treated with milacemide. Milace- 
mide and its metabolite, glycine, may have no role 
in the treatment of myoclonus, stiff-person syn- 
drome, or the other diseases studied, or the dose 
may have been insufficient to increase glycine lev- 
els in the brain.

The glycine receptor is involved in urea-induced 
myoclonus (3). Whole-brain and brainstem glycine 
levels are decreased in DDT-induced myoclonus in 
mice and rats (43). Intraventricular glycine sup- 
presses DDT-induced myoclonus (6). 
Animal models of myoclonus, implicating glycin- 
ergic dysfunction led Truong and Fahn (7) to try 
glycine in patients with myoclonus; however, gly- 
cine in doses up to 6 g/day was unsuccessful in the 
treatment of myoclonus. CSF glycine levels did not 
change during treatment; this finding suggested that 
this dose did not effectively enter the brain. Animal 
studies had previously shown that glycine does not 
easily cross the blood-brain barrier (8,9). 
Milacemide (2-n-pentylaminoacetamide), rnanu- 
factured by Searle, is a prodrug of glycine. Milace- 
mide readily penetrates the blood-brain barrier; in 
the brain; it is metabolized by monoamine oxi- 
dase-B (MAO-B) to glycineamide and then to gly- 
cine (10). In rats, systemic administration of mila- 
cemide blocks the myoclonus induced by DDT (1 1) 
as effectively as glycine infused into the ventricles 
(6). Glycine levels in the brain increase with admin- 
istration of milacemide, but serine levels do not 
change. Therefore, increasing brain glycine levels, 
484

MILACEMIDE IN MYOCLONUS 485 
either by systemic administration of milacemide or 
by intraventricular infusion of glycine, may be a 
mechanism to produce an antimyoclonic effect. It is 
not clear if milacemide, while preventing myoclo- 
nus in the DDT model, could also do so via seroto- 
nin neurotransmission since it inhibits MAO-B ac- 
tivity (12-14). Milacemide also increases y-ami- 
nobutyric acid (GABA) concentrations in the 
substantia nigra (10). 
Milacemide has an acceptable safety profile in 
animals (10). In humans, milacemide has been eval- 
uated for safety in healthy volunteers. Milacemide 
has been relatively well-tolerated in therapeutic tri- 
als conducted in patients with epilepsy (15). Ad- 
verse effects may include vasomotor disorders 
(flushing), nausea and vomiting, palpitations, and 
elevations in hepatic transaminases (10). These ab- 
normalities generally return to normal following 
cessation of drug or reduction of dosage (10). 
Since glycine, GABA, and the monoamines are 
major inhibitory neurotransmitters in the CNS, mi- 
lacemide may be a potential agent in the therapy of 
myoclonus and other movement disorders. Brown 
et al. (16), in an open-label trial of milacemide ti- 
trated to 2,400 mglday in seven subjects with my- 
oclonus and three with stiff-person syndrome, 
found no significant improvement. We report a trial 
of milacemide in nine patients with intractable 
movement disorders. 
METHODS 
Milacemide was obtained from Searle (Skokie, 
IL, U.S.A.). The study was approved by the Insti- 
tutional Review Board, and written informed con- 
sent was obtained from each subject enrolled. 
The study had three phases. Phase I was an open- 
label dose-titration lead-in, beginning at a dosage of 
800 mg, orally, three times a day, and not exceeding 
1,600 mg three times a day (4,800 mglday). During 
Phase I, patients who did not respond or who ex- 
perienced significant treatment-related adverse 
events were withdrawn. Phase I1 was a double- 
blind, randomized design that employed the optimal 
dose determined in Phase I or a matching placebo at 
the same dose. Subjects were transferred immedi- 
ately from Phase I to Phase 11, without gradual 
withdrawal of drug. Phase 111 was similar to Phase 
11, without gradual withdrawal of drug. Phase 111 
was similar to Phase 11, with the blinded treatment 
reversed. The study was terminated when the max- 
imal duration of treatment in Phase I11 was attained. 
Subjects could participate as inpatients or outpa- 
tients. In Phase I, dose titration occurred over 12 
days for inpatients and over 21 days for outpatients, 
followed by 1 week of treatment at the optimal 
dose. In Phase I1 and Phase 111, inpatients received 
milacemide or placebo for 1 week and outpatients 
received milacemide or placebo for 3 weeks. 
Potential subjects were men or nonpregnant 
women (either sterile or using adequate contracep- 
tives) between the ages of 18 and 90 years who suf- 
fered from myoclonus or another intractable move- 
ment disorder and who were otherwise in good 
health. For at least 30 days before enrollment, sub- 
jects were on a stable regimen of any drugs used to 
treat their myoclonus or other movement disorder. 
Patients with serious medical conditions or labora- 
tory abnormalities, recent histories of alcohol or 
drug abuse, other concurrent or recent investiga- 
tional drug studies, known hypersensitivity to mi- 
lacemide, or previous participation in this study 
were excluded. 
Screening was performed within 14 days of en- 
rollment and included informed consent, medical 
history, physical and neurologic examination, elec- 
trocardiogram, laboratory tests (complete blood 
count, electrolytes, liver functions, urine analysis, 
and pregnancy test), videotape, and assessment of 
severity. Global assessment was on a four-point 
scale: 0, no signs; 1, mild signs, not interfering with 
activities; 2, moderate signs, interfering with some 
activities; 3, severe signs, interfering with many ac- 
tivities; and 4, marked signs, interfering with most 
activities. Ratings were done by the subjects, family 
members, and treating physicians. Laboratories 
tests were repeated during the study and obtained at 
the end of each phase. 
Ten subjects were enrolled: six with myoclonus 
of various etiologies and four others with intracta- 
ble movement disorders (one each with progressive 
supranuclear palsy, Filipino x-linked dystonia with 
parkinsonism, painful legs and moving toes, and 
stiff-person syndrome; Table 1).

age 16, has a history of congenital right hemiparesis

His clinical picture has been described previously

MILACEMIDE IN MYOCLONUS 487 
RESULTS 
The clinical rating score did not change signifi- 
cantly in nine patients treated with milacemide. 
Only one (case 6, with presumed cortical-basal gan- 
glionic degeneration) had some apparent benefit 
with less severe myoclonus in the open-label trial. 
He continued through Phase I1 and Phase I11 with- 
out clear benefit. 
Eight of the I0 subjects completed Phase I (the 
open trial) to a maximum dose of 4,800 mglday. 
Two patients withdrew from the study due to side 
effects at 3,600 mglday without any benefit. A pa- 
tient (case 3) with rhythmic myoclonus experienced 
excessive appetite. The patient (case 8) with painful 
legs and moving toes had a transient exacerbation 
of her condition. Both side effects resolved after 
discontinuation of milacemide. 
Full blood counts, electrolytes, and liver function 
tests did not change significantly. 
DISCUSSION 
The 10 subjects in our study did not benefit from 
milacemide in doses up to 4,800 mg/day. Brown et 
al. (16), in an open-label trial of milacemide titrated 
to 2,400 mg/day in seven subjects with myoclonus 
and three with stiff-man syndrome, also found no 
significant improvement. 
The inhibitory neurotransmitter, glycine, was un- 
successful in the treatment of myoclonus in doses 
up to 6 g/day (7), possibly due to poor penetration of 
glycine into the brain from the peripheral circula- 
tion. However, milacemide, a glycine precursor 
known to readily cross the blood-brain barrier, did 
not improve the myoclonus in the six myoclonus 
patients in this study or in the seven patients pre- 
viously studied (16). It is possible that the dose of 
milacemide was too low to sufficiently increase gly- 
cine levels in the CNS. However, the ineffective- 
ness of milacemide in these cases of myoclonus 
may suggest that defective glycinergic neurotrans- 
mission is not an important factor in myoclonus. 
Precise mechanisms for the various types of myoc- 
lonus are not known. Posthypoxic myoclonus may 
involve serotonergic (21,22) and GABA-ergic (23) 
neurotransmission, as suggested by reduced CSF 
levels of 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (SHIAA), the 
major metabolite of serotonin, and of GABA. Post- 
anoxic myoclonus improves with drugs that en- 
hance serotonin activity [such as L-~-HTP, the im- 
mediate synthetic precursor to serotonin; tryp- 
tophan with a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (22); or 
fluoxetine, an inhibitor of serotonin reuptake (24)] 
and also with drugs, such as valproic acid and clo- 
nazepam, that enhance GABA-ergic inhibitory in- 
fluence (21,25). 
Brown et al. (16) postulated that the discrepancy 
between the effectiveness of glycine and milace- 
mide in improving DDT-induced myoclonus and 
their ineffectiveness in treating myoclonus in hu- 
mans may be due to the fact that animal experi- 
ments for myoclonus involve manipulation of the 
reticular formation and thus may not be an appro- 
priate model for cortical and spinal myoclonus. 
However, our case 2 is believed to have reticular 
reflex myoclonus (18), and she failed to improve. 
Defective glycinergic systems have been impli- 
cated in some animal models of spinal rigidity 
(26,27). Schmidt et al. (28) noted that the rigidity in 
stiff-person syndrome resembles that produced by 
strychnine poisoning and experimental cord isch- 
emia, both of which are associated with a loss of 
normal glycinergic inhibition to motoneurons from 
spinal interneurons. This observation provoked 
speculation that abnormalities in glycinergic inhibi- 
tion by spinal interneurons might play a role in stiff- 
person syndrome (28). Trials of glycine in stiff- 
person syndrome (28,29) were not successful, 
possibly because of the poor penetration of the 
blood-brain barrier by glycine (7). 
There is more evidence for an imbalance in the 
GABA-ergic system in stiff-person syndrome. Med- 
ications with GABA-ergic properties, such as diaz- 
epam (30), valproic acid (31), clonazepam (32), and 
baclofen (33,34), are beneficial in some patients. 
Antibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase, the 
enzyme that synthesizes GABA, are present in the 
serum and CSF of many stiff-person patients 
(35,36). 
We offer two possible explanations for the lack of 
benefit in subjects treated with milacemide. Milace- 
mide and its metabolite, glycine, may have no role 
in the treatment of myoclonus, stiff-person syn- 
drome, or the other diseases studied, or the dose 
may have been insufficient to increase glycine lev- 
els in the brain.
